payload.name: Store Explicit Counts for Enumerated Sets
payload.description: When constructing memories from a message that introduces or names a new member of a countable set (e.g., pets, children, vehicles) and the full set is explicitly enumerated in the conversation, include the explicit total count in the extracted candidate or memory update.
content: During extraction, when a message names a new member of a countable set (pets, children, vehicles, etc.) and the conversation explicitly enumerates all current members, include the explicit total count in the candidate content, not just the individual member.

During CRUD, when ADDing or UPDATEing a memory that describes a set of named items, ensure the stored content contains the explicit aggregate count if the source conversation supports it; do not rely on the reader to count separate memories.

candidates.solves: Future questions asking 'how many' of a person's countable possessions (pets, children, vehicles) fail when memory contains individual named entries but no explicit total. The diagnosed cause is extraction recording each new member without synthesizing the aggregate count, even when the conversation enumerates the complete set. The reusable rule is to store the explicit total whenever all members are named in the source; it does not apply when the set is only partially mentioned or the count must be guessed.

payload.name: Preserve explicit adjectives in memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a statement in which the speaker explicitly describes a subject with a specific adjective, keep that exact descriptor in the candidate memory content.
content: During extraction or update, if the source directly describes a subject with an explicit adjective or qualifier, include that exact adjective in the memory content. Do not replace precise evaluative words with broader paraphrases or implications. Only include descriptors that are explicitly supported by the source; do not infer unstated ones.

candidates.solves: When a source explicitly applies an adjective to a subject, extraction can drop that specific descriptor while keeping a broader implication, so later factual questions miss the exact claim. Preserve explicitly stated evaluative adjectives in the memory content rather than replacing them with paraphrase. This applies to any future extraction where a speaker directly characterizes something; it does not require inferring descriptors not stated.

payload.name: Extract exact object of missing or longing
payload.description: When a speaker says they miss, long for, or are nostalgic about something and then states the specific aspect in an exclamation or follow-up phrase, before creating or updating a memory ensure that exact aspect is included.
content: During extraction, if a speaker expresses missing or longing for an activity, identify the exact noun phrase they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments') and record it as the object, not just the broader activity summary. Include any clarifying exclamation that follows. When updating or merging, preserve this specific object rather than replacing it with a generic paraphrase.

candidates.solves: When a speaker says they miss an activity but does not name any specific aspect, a concise activity summary is sufficient. The failure occurs when the speaker follows with an exclamation naming a precise thing they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments'), and the extraction keeps only the broad activity, losing the exact object. This skill adds the rule to capture the specific noun phrase from the exclamation as the object of missing. Future sessions with 'miss', 'long for', or 'nostalgic' statements that clarify a particular aspect will benefit. It does not apply when no specific aspect is named.

payload.name: Separate speaker-specific feelings during extraction
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when multiple speakers share personal feelings or reactions in a conversation; create separate memories per speaker instead of merging them.
content: During extraction, when one speaker states their own feeling or inspiration and another speaker then shares a different feeling or reaction, create a separate candidate memory for each speaker's self-attributed statement.
Do not merge the second speaker's response into the first speaker's memory; preserve the exact speaker as the subject of each 'I feel' or 'I think' statement.
If a memory candidate aggregates multiple turns, verify that every distinct speaker's claim is represented in its own candidate before deciding to add.

candidates.solves: A construction extraction failure occurred when one speaker's feeling was captured but another speaker's contrasting feeling in the same exchange was dropped, leaving later questions about the second speaker unanswerable. The reusable rule is to extract each participant's self-attributed feeling as its own memory during multi-turn conversations, preserving speaker boundaries. This applies to any multi-party dialogue where feelings, preferences, or opinions are exchanged.

payload.name: Preserve Direct Answers in Extraction
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about how they learned or acquired a skill, include that answer as a distinct fact during extraction and keep it when updating an existing memory.
content: During extraction, list every discrete factual statement in a message; do not omit facts merely because they do not match the main theme of an existing memory.

When a message directly answers a question about how, when, or from whom the speaker learned a skill, always capture that answer (e.g., self-taught, taught by someone, learned at a certain age) as part of the candidate content.

When updating an existing memory, preserve all newly stated details in the enriched content or create an additional candidate; do not select just the facts that expand the current memory and drop the direct answer.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often keep only facts that align with an existing memory theme and silently drop other directly stated facts, such as how someone learned a skill (self-taught vs taught). This matters when a later question asks about that dropped fact. The Skill instructs extraction to capture every discrete fact from a message, especially direct answers to questions about acquisition or ability, and to preserve those facts when enriching an existing memory.

payload.name: Extract nickname relationships from address terms
payload.description: When a dialogue message contains a speaker addressing another person by a name that differs from the addressee's full name, extract a nickname relationship even if the message's main topic is an event.
content: During extraction, scan direct-address terms (greetings, vocatives) in each message and compare them against the full names of the conversation participants.
When a direct-address term is a shortened or alternative form of a participant's full name, create a relationship memory recording that the speaker uses that term as a nickname for that participant.
Add this nickname relationship independently of any event/state memory extracted from the same message; do not drop address terms because another fact seems more salient.

candidates.solves: The construction extraction step can over-focus on a message's main event and discard direct-address nicknames as incidental, leaving later nickname queries unanswerable. The reusable fix is to treat any non-full-name address term as an independent relationship fact during extraction. This applies to future dialogue where a nickname appears in a greeting or vocative; it does not apply to generic pronouns, formal titles, or address terms matching the full name.

payload.name: Preserve all distinct claims in multi-claim utterances
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from an utterance that describes multiple distinct activities, hobbies, or topics each with its own value, feeling, or outcome, ensure each distinct claim is preserved.
content: During candidate extraction, treat an utterance containing multiple independent claims as a set of distinct memory candidates; do not let one salient claim suppress another.
If combining claims into one memory, include every subject and its specific predicate; if any claim cannot be combined cleanly, emit a separate ADD candidate so all evidence-backed facts survive.

candidates.solves: A speaker utterance describes multiple distinct activities or topics, each with its own evaluation or benefit, and extraction preserves only the most salient claim, losing other evidence-backed facts. This skill applies whenever constructing memories from multi-claim utterances in any future session, regardless of topic, and does not require knowing the gold answer.

payload.name: CaptureDirectDisclosureRecipient
payload.description: When a user directly tells a conversation partner about a personal life event, extract the act of telling that partner as a durable fact, not just the event itself.
content: During extraction, if a message is a direct address (e.g., 'Hey Sam, ...') and the speaker discloses a personal event (marriage, job, move, health, etc.), create a memory that records both the event and that the speaker informed that specific addressee.
Do not drop the addressee as conversational framing; later questions may ask who was told.
Do not apply this to generic statements, third-party news, or non-durable small talk.

candidates.solves: The failure was an extraction candidate that captured a marriage announcement but omitted that the speaker told Sam, so later memory could not answer 'who did X tell?'. This skill applies whenever a directly addressed disclosure of a personal event occurs, and requires recording the recipient of the disclosure. It does not apply to third-party statements or non-durable routine small talk.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-evaluative experience statements
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about their own recent experience with an overall assessment and specific positive/negative details, use during candidate extraction to capture the explicit statement as a memory candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message explicitly describes the speaker's own recent experience, outcome, or season with an overall assessment and supporting positive/negative details, create a memory candidate for that description; do not skip it merely because it is conversational or mixed in sentiment.
Preserve the key facts and the overall assessment in the candidate, and include any concrete outcome (e.g., a win or loss) as part of the same or a linked event candidate when available.

candidates.solves: Construction failed because an explicit first-person evaluative statement answering a question about the speaker's own team season was not extracted as a candidate, so no memory was persisted. The abstract mechanism is missing extraction of direct self-reports that combine an overall assessment with specific positives/negatives. This rule applies to future sessions where a user or assistant characterizes their own experience, project, or outcome in response to a question; it does not cover inferring unstated opinions or summarizing third-party facts.

payload.name: Extract reported third-party condition assessments
payload.description: When a message contains a third-party reported assessment (e.g., doctor's statement) about a person's condition, use during extraction to create a state memory for the assessed person.
content: During extraction, if a speaker reports what a third party (doctor, specialist, etc.) said about someone's condition, create a `state` candidate about the person whose condition is assessed. Include the assessment and date/session time when known.
Keep this as a separate candidate even when the same message also expresses support or describes the speaker's own situation.
Resolve the assessed subject from the conversation context, not from the current speaker, and apply this to any reported evaluation.

candidates.solves: During construction, a speaker often relays a third party's assessment of someone's condition (e.g., 'doctor said not serious') inside a supportive reply, and extraction can miss it by focusing on the speaker's own state or on mutual support. Use this to extract reported evaluations as durable state facts about the person discussed. Applies to any reported authoritative evaluation; not retrieval-side answer selection.

payload.name: Preserve Direct Speaker Statements in Memories
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker's direct statement or quotation to another person, ensure extracted or updated memory content includes the speaker's words and attribution, not just the listener's reaction.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a direct quote or specific statement from a speaker about an event, plan, or relationship, preserve the speaker's words (or close paraphrase) and the speaker's identity in the memory candidate, rather than summarizing only the listener's reaction or the event from the listener's perspective.
When updating existing memories, if a new message includes a speaker's direct statement that adds a fact or quote not yet stored, incorporate that statement with its speaker attribution.

candidates.solves: Construction candidates often summarize an exchange from the listener's perspective, omitting the speaker's direct words (e.g., a quote) and attributing the sentiment to the wrong person. This rule abstracts the failure to require preserving speaker identity and quoted content when a message contains a clear statement, and applies to future sessions where a specific person says something memorable or plan-relevant.

payload.name: Preserve co-participants in extracted events
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message reports an event shared by the speaker and another person using inclusive phrases (e.g., 'we', 'my partner and I', 'my friend and I'); extract the memory with all participants included.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source message describes an event or activity involving multiple people through inclusive phrases such as 'we', 'my partner and I', or 'my friend and I', include every named or clearly implied participant in the extracted content.
Do not reduce a plural subject to only the speaker; preserve the joint nature of the event even if the other participant is not named again in later messages.
When another participant is not explicitly named, record their role or relationship (e.g., 'with partner', 'with friend') instead of omitting them from the event memory.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction omitted the speaker's travel companion from a joint event memory, so later queries about the companion were unsupported. The abstract mechanism is that extraction summaries often collapse first-person plural statements ('my partner and I', 'we') into the speaker alone. This rule applies to future construction extraction whenever a message reports an activity shared with others, instructing the system to preserve all named or clearly implied participants. It does not apply to CRUD operations or solo-activity memories.

payload.name: Extract third-party progress praise statements
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker makes an explicit evaluative statement about another person's progress, achievement, or effort, create a memory candidate preserving the speaker's claim.
content: During extraction, treat a speaker's evaluative statement about a specific other person's progress, achievement, or effort as a candidate fact attributable to the speaker, even when phrased as praise or encouragement (e.g., 'your hard work is paying off').
Record the target person and the claimed state/outcome as a compact state or relationship memory, linked to the speaker's utterance as evidence.
Do not skip such statements because they are complimentary or because the target is not the speaker.

candidates.solves: Messages where one person explicitly assesses another's progress are often skipped as mere praise, so later queries about 'what did X say about Y's progress?' fail. This skill makes extraction preserve such speaker-attributed evaluative statements. Applies to any named third party and progress comments; not to generic aphorisms without a specific subject or internal plans.

payload.name: Extract-multiple-independent-facts-per-message
payload.description: When a message or conversational turn contains independent durable facts about more than one person or topic, use this during extraction to create a separate candidate for each fact instead of keeping only one.
content: During candidate extraction, scan the full message for every clause that states a distinct durable fact (event, achievement, preference, state) about any person; create one candidate per fact, even when a reply mentions another person's activity.

When two speakers' facts appear in one exchange (e.g., one person reports an achievement and the other mentions their own trip), do not choose one subject; emit separate event/state memories for each.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction failures in construction when a single message or exchange contains independent durable facts about more than one person. The diagnosed cause was that extraction recorded only Joanna's road trip and omitted Nate's explicitly stated video game tournament win. The rule to enumerate each distinct fact as a separate candidate generalizes to any future multi-fact message, and it does not apply to CRUD operations or to merging related details.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Social Interaction Events
payload.description: When a message explicitly states a social interaction (e.g., skyped, met, talked, visited) with a person and what was discussed or shared, create an extraction candidate for the interaction and topic.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly mentions that someone interacted with another person (by skype, meeting, talk, visit, etc.) and states the topic or shared content, create an event or relationship candidate with the participants, action, topic, and any stated time.
Do not skip such a candidate simply because the interaction is mentioned in casual conversation; record it when it is specific enough to answer a future question about the interaction.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a message explicitly reporting a social interaction (skyped with a fan, discussed characters) produced no extraction candidate, so the fact was never stored. The abstract failure is that explicit interaction statements with a topic can be overlooked during candidate extraction. This rule applies to any future message that states an interaction between people and its topic, and where that fact might later be queried.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitMediaFactsDuringExtraction
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message states a concrete fact about a shared photo, video, or other media (e.g., location, date, subject) while also containing general commentary; preserve the factual detail explicitly.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a concrete fact about shared media (e.g., where or when a photo was taken, who is in it), create a candidate that states that fact directly; do not let a broader discussion/theme candidate replace it.
When a message mixes factual detail with reflective commentary, store the factual claim separately from any general theme; both may be valid memories, but the fact must not be omitted.
Before accepting an ADD candidate, check that every directly stated factual detail that could answer a future question is retained; a candidate that only restates the topic is incomplete.

candidates.solves: Concrete factual details about shared media (e.g., a photo's location) are often lost when extraction creates only a general discussion memory. This rule requires preserving such explicit facts as standalone candidates whenever a message mixes a factual statement with commentary. Applies to any media-related fact (location, time, subject); not to purely opinion/theme summaries.

payload.name: Infer writing from online forum discussion
payload.description: Apply during extraction when a user mentions joining or participating in an online forum/community and describes talking, discussing, or chatting about topics; record that they write comments/posts on those topics.
content: If a user says they joined or participate in an online forum/community and mentions talking, discussing, or chatting about subjects, extract an event memory stating they write comments/posts on those subjects, not just that they participated or talked.
Do not apply if the user explicitly indicates reading only, lurking, or offline conversations.
Preserve the subject and topics from the message exactly; use memory kind 'event', and set subject to the user.

candidates.solves: The extraction step omitted the writing aspect of a user's participation in an online forum, recording only that they joined and discussed topics. This skill ensures that when a user mentions discussing/talking in an online forum or community, the memory includes that they write comments/posts on those topics, because online forum discussions are written communications. It applies to any future message where forum/community participation is described with discussion verbs.

payload.name: Extract subject facts from partner confirmations
payload.description: When a conversational partner refers to something the subject shared or did and names or describes it, extract a memory for the subject from that confirming detail.
content: During extraction, consider messages from all participants as potential evidence about the subject, not only the subject's own statements.

If a reply names, labels, or describes something the subject shared or did in a prior message, generate a candidate event memory for the subject that includes that concrete detail, grounded in both the original message and the confirming reply.
Do not let the absence of the subject's own explicit label prevent extraction when a partner's direct attribution supplies it.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often ignores factual claims made by a conversational partner about the subject, especially when the partner comments on media or an activity the subject shared (e.g., labeling a posted meal). This causes missing memories. The proposed rule directs extraction to treat direct third-party attributions as candidate evidence for subject events, so future sessions capture facts that are only stated by the other speaker.

payload.name: Preserve Companion in Shared Activity Extraction
payload.description: When constructing memories from conversation and a user describes an activity or preference with 'we', 'us', or 'together', retrieve this Skill to ensure the companion and shared activity are captured.
content: During extraction, when a message uses first-person plural ('we', 'us', 'our') or 'together' to express an activity or preference, create a candidate that names the companion (if identifiable from conversation) and the shared activity.
Do not merge the shared activity only into a memory about the speaker alone; preserve it as a joint activity with the companion, using 'event' or 'relationship' memory kind as appropriate.
If the companion is not explicit, use the most recent person the speaker was discussing or leave the companion as the implied co-participant rather than dropping it.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the activity when a speaker uses first-person plural, losing the companion and the relational fact. This Skill addresses that by requiring the companion and shared activity to be extracted together, enabling future questions about joint activities. It applies to any conversation where activities or preferences are expressed with 'we' or 'together'.

payload.name: Extract distinct factual claims from multi-turn dialogue
payload.description: When constructing memories from a multi-turn conversation, if a speaker states a specific effect or personal fact (e.g., how an activity makes them feel), extract it as its own memory instead of merging it into a broad conversation summary.
content: During extraction, parse each speaker turn for explicit self-referential claims (activities, feelings, preferences, routines). Create a separate memory for each such claim, using the speaker as subject and the appropriate memory kind (e.g., preference or state).

Do not reduce a multi-topic conversation to a single event memory that only lists discussed topics; ensure every explicit factual statement with lasting relevance is represented in its own memory entry.
If a claim is made in response to a question, still treat it as a durable stated belief and record it independently.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure is that the construction agent collapsed a multi-turn conversation into one event summary, omitting an explicit statement that exercise makes the speaker feel connected to her body. The reusable problem is extraction over-summarization: any time a conversation contains multiple distinct self-disclosures, a single event memory cannot preserve them. This rule applies to future multi-turn dialogues where speakers state specific effects, preferences, or routines, and directs the agent to emit one memory per durable claim.
